title: Why Has CEO Pay Increased So Much?
research_question: What explains the dramatic rise in CEO pay in the United States over recent decades, and what accounts for differences in CEO compensation across firms of different sizes and across countries? Specifically, to what extent can the level and growth of executive compensation be attributed to the size of firms that CEOs manage versus other factors such as governance failures or rent extraction?
data_description: The study combines several data sources. CEO compensation data come from ExecuComp (1992–2004), using the TDC1 measure (salary, bonus, restricted stock, and Black–Scholes value of options granted) for the top 500–1,000 paid CEOs. Longer time-series compensation data come from Jensen, Murphy, and Wruck (covering S&P 500 CEOs from 1970) and Frydman and Saks (covering top three officers in 50 large firms at 1940, 1960, 1990 benchmarks, extended through 2003). Firm-level data on market capitalization (debt plus equity), EBIT, and sales come from Compustat (1978–2004). Governance data use the Gompers–Ishii–Metrick index. Cross-country compensation data come from a 2002 Towers Perrin survey covering 17 countries, with firm size proxied by median net income of the top 50 firms from Compustat Global. Nominal values are deflated using the BEA GDP deflator. Unit of observation is the firm-year (or country in cross-country analysis).
institutional_context: Between 1980 and 2003, average compensation of large-firm U.S. CEOs rose roughly sixfold in real terms, sparking public controversy and debate over whether the increase reflects efficient market forces, weakened corporate governance and managerial rent extraction, or shifts in pay structure toward stock options and high-powered incentives. Over the same period, the market capitalization of large U.S. firms also grew approximately sixfold, raising the question of whether expanding firm scale mechanically increases the productivity and equilibrium price of top managerial talent. The setting features a competitive market in which heterogeneous CEOs are matched to heterogeneous firms, with the largest firms attracting the most talented managers because talent's marginal impact scales with firm size. Cross-country variation in firm size, segmented national executive labor markets, and differences in corporate governance quality provide additional variation for examining how aggregate firm value translates into executive pay levels.
